Is this worthy of a GH issue in Charter for an agent to check on and purpose to the user as a ::question if said deferral isn't covered already in a GH issue?

anchor.quote: No override, no --force, no autonomy dial.

body: On re-attempts where the model choice has hit the ceiling because of costly: true and where a stronger model would have been chosen had costly: false been set, then a strong warning should be logged, so a reviewer (human or agent)  knows that a failure may be due to a limited model's thinking ability.
But bumps can cross model providers, right?  A bump may go from running a local model to using Claude Opus for example.  Right?
If a human indicated to use a costly model for a task, then a costly judge can be used without a halt or further questioning of the user.

anchor.quote: A hard task whose only capable block is costly: true fails

body: Only fails after all its attempts have been expended.  For example, if the first attempt run with Opus and Fable is costly, and it would have been chosen in a re-attempt of the task, then Opus will run over and over until all attempts have been exhausted.  A premature halt here after the first attempt because the task was considered too hard for Opus, doesn't give Opus a chance that might succeed in part because of the extra prompting a re-attempt gets about its failure in the previous attempt.
A /plan-breakdown, can (and should if warranted) recommend to the user to use a costly model for certain tasks.

Checked, and all three are genuinely backlogged rather than only recorded here: #227 (probes), #228 (ladder), #231 (steering) are all OPEN, as are #229 and #230. So no orphaned deferral in this plan. Your second point is the better one and I have filed it: Charter #156 - an authoring agent should verify that every deferral a plan names is covered by a tracked issue, and raise a :::question when nothing tracks it. I argued there that Charter should NOT grow issue-tracker integration; the binary stays dependency-free and the agent does the lookup, which also makes it work for non-GitHub trackers. I am adding the issue numbers to the scope note here so the plan itself carries them.

Accepted, and added to the plan. A binding costly ceiling is currently invisible: the resolver silently returns the weaker block and a subsequent failure looks like an ordinary failure, so nobody can tell whether the model simply lacked the reasoning to finish. The warning does not weaken the costly floor at all, because it changes what is LOGGED, never what is SELECTED. Note this is an addition to the design of record rather than a restatement of it: DoR 6.2 specifies the exclusion but no surfacing for it, so this needs to land as an amendment in #342. I have flagged it in the plan as such.

Yes, and that is the intended case rather than a side effect. Candidates(R) is computed over EVERY block in the registry regardless of kind, and the only ordering axis is ascending strength, so a bump from a local block to a Claude block is exactly what the rule produces when the local model is the weak actor. Nothing in the predicate mentions the provider. The one caveat is the costly floor: if the stronger Claude block is marked costly:true it is excluded, and per DoR 6.5 point 5 the judge stays at the actor route and fires the advisory instead - which is precisely the case your other note amends. Since you had to ask, an implementer would too, so I have made it explicit in the plan.

Accepted as a ruling, and it is a real change rather than a clarification, so I want to be explicit about what it moves. DoR 6.5 point 5 currently says the judge bump obeys the costly floor unconditionally: if the only stronger block is costly, the judge stays at the actor route and fires the advisory. Your rule adds that human sanction PROPAGATES - once a human has pinned a costly model for the actor, costly spend is already sanctioned for that task, so the judge may bump into a costly block without a halt or a further prompt. That is coherent with the floor as stated, because the floor constrains the HARNESS choosing, never the human assigning, and the human has already assigned here. It does need to land as an amendment to 6.5 point 5 in #342 rather than as plan-only text, otherwise the next implementer reads the DoR and reverts it. Folded into the plan and flagged as an amendment.

I think this one is a misreading that my wording invited, so let me separate the two halves rather than just agree. The acceptance line is about VALIDATE time, not run time: GR2048 refuses the config before the run starts, at zero spend, when a used tier has no non-costly block at or above it. It is not a mid-run halt after attempt one and it never interrupts a task that has a capable block. On your scenario specifically: in v1 there is NO escalation at all. The resolver is a pure function of (tag + registry), so it returns the same block on every attempt. Opus running over and over across the full retry budget, collecting the extra prompting each re-attempt gets, is exactly what v1 does - your concern is already the shipped behaviour, and there is no premature-halt path that could pre-empt it. The underlying principle is still valuable, but it lands on v2: when the ladder (#228) can graduate a task mid-run, it must not escalate before the retry budget is spent, because retry feedback is itself a lever and escalating early buys a stronger model while throwing away the cheaper fix. I will record that on #228. And since the acceptance line misread once, I am rewording it to say validate-time explicitly.

Accepted, and it fits the floor rather than bending it: the harness recommending a costly model and a human assigning one are different acts, and only the second is a selection. This is the constructive counterpart to the halt - instead of only refusing to choose costly, the breakdown can tell you WHERE costly is warranted and let you pin it. It is skill-side work (plan-breakdown) rather than resolver work, so it does not belong in this stage scope; I am recording it in the plan as a follow-up and will file it against the tagging doctrine (#225 / #229 area) so it does not become the untracked deferral your first note warned about.

Agreed - Charter should not grow issue-tracker integration, and keeping the binary dependency-free is the right call. I want the Charter agent team to hold this while working the issue, so it is now recorded as a maintainer ruling at the TOP of #156 rather than sitting as one of the open design questions at the bottom.
